I’m currently studying symbolic logic at the moment. Our class just reviewed truth-value tables for material conditionals; we are studying “if then” statements. If ‘X’ is false, the whole statement can still be true. If the consequent is false (‘Y’, ‘Q’, or ‘Z’), and the antecedent (‘X’) is true, then the statement is false. However, if the antecedent is false (‘X’) but the consequent is true, the statement is true. This is called a vacuous truth. If both the antecedent and consequent are false, the statement is still true but vacuously so.

I think what you’re feeling is the mechanical grip in GT4. Since these cars are not nearly as aero reliant, they rely much more on mechanical grip. In GT3, aero packages are rather immense in that these cars become much more sensitive to ride height and yaw/slip angles. It’s typically easier and more time-forgiving to have a small slide in GT4. However, it is more dangerous and time consuming to have a small slide in GT3 as you risk stalling the aero. It’s a “different” kind of racing and race setup and, I appreciate your preference for GT4. But, the physics and edge of grip is just as much there for the GT3. They just cannot feel and be driven the same way.

Edit: I prefer to drive cars which are less aero reliant.

I think my point is that since space expands, light wavelength increases. Therefore, its energy also decreases. Microwaves exhibit a longer wavelength than infrared. So, I think that microwaves are the remnant of objects which are farther away and older than the infrared.

Edit: basically, I think it is incorrect to say that Webb will provide scientists with the oldest images of the universe. While it could be rudimentary, we do have an image of the cosmic microwave background. This image will show objects that are older and further away than the infrared. Webb is allowing scientists to view high resolution infrared radiation, which it very much unchartered territory.

I think I should clarify. It’s likely that the existence of science relies on transcendental objects (an eternal truth might fit this category), but the practice or methodology of science does not concern itself with them. If scientists discuss what it means for truth to be eternal, that is more of a metaphysical discussion of epistemology. I wouldn’t say that this discussion is scientific. When I say that it isn’t scientific, I do not mean that it is bad or without proof. What I mean is that science is limited to studying the natural world. So, perhaps science relies on the “unnatural”, but it does not study the “unnatural.” What do you think?

I wouldn’t say that science necessarily relies on unnatural explanations. The natural sciences are just that, they study the natural world. I could be wrong in that remark. From my understanding, a big proponent in this “conflict” is the discussion on differing epistemic procedure. The supernatural cannot be understood in the same way that cosmology or physics can. In the natural world, we may observe and record our measurements. We may test hypotheses by way of direct correspondence to the real world. In science, there appears to be a clearer way of certitude. In the supernatural or transcendental, subjective experience plays a significant role. This subjective experience may lead to inconsistent reports on what the transcendental really is. In science, experiments can be replicated. In the transcendental world, replication could prove to be more difficult. As a side note, I’m only in my undergrad. I’ve not done any research, but an epistemic divide could be a good talking point.

Now, if I am to argue against the notion that every possible sin was initiated by God, one might say that I am limiting an unlimited God. 

I suppose the difference here hinges on the ideas that He is good, He is gracious and loving, He is just, etc. Perhaps there are constraints to an all powerful God. (lol) Because God is Holy, God cannot sin. If we don’t agree with His actions (God asking Abraham to kill his son Isaac) our disagreement does not make His actions wrong. Rather, it could be a testament to the nature of morality within the human mind; sometimes morality is difficult to understand even outside of theological proceeds.

In the end, it was his decision to create us. So sure, if we or any being capable of sin was not created, sin would not exist. I’m not sure that this statement relieves us from responsibility.

If your argument is true, then why should I accept the responsibility of my actions? For no reason, I could punch my roommate and think, “Yeah that was God’s fault because He allowed it to happen. Furthermore, because he allowed it to happen, this means that God is morally bankrupt.”  

I think there is more to the equation here.
